summary:
Arkansas stands under the United States national framework on travel documents. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary and barred self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and the Supreme Court in November 2025 allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect.

Arkansas itself carries a heavy state-level legal burden. The July 2026 anti-trans national legal risk assessment map places Arkansas in its "Worst Policies In Effect" group, one tier below the four "Do Not Travel" states (Florida, Idaho, Kansas, Texas). Arkansas's own risk profile rests on a cluster of enacted and enforceable restrictions rather than pending proposals.

Bathroom and facilities access is restricted. Act 619, signed 21 March 2023 and effective immediately, barred trans people from using public school bathrooms matching their gender identity, making Arkansas the fourth state to do so. A separate Act 619, which became law 11 April 2023, created a misdemeanor for trans use of public bathrooms, locker rooms or changing facilities where a minor is present, dependent on intent of arousing or gratifying sexual desire. The Movement Advancement Project's equality-map citations record HB 1156 as a 2023 K-12 facility ban extended in 2025.

Gender-affirming care for minors is banned. Arkansas was the first state to enact such a ban, in 2021, after the legislature overrode the governor's veto of HB 1570, which prohibited puberty blockers, hormone therapy and surgery for under-18s. A federal judge initially blocked the law for "irreparable harm" to minors and struck it down 20 June 2023 for discrimination and constitutional violations, but on 12 August 2025 the Eighth Circuit overturned that ruling and allowed enforcement, citing United States v. Skrmetti. Litigation over the 2021 care ban continues.

Trans athletes are barred from school sports. A law signed 25 March 2021 and effective immediately prohibits transgender women and girls from competing on school sports teams consistent with their gender identity across K-12 and collegiate sports, and allows a student or school claiming harm to sue for violation.

State identity documents are mixed. Arkansas has permitted transgender people to amend birth certificates since 1981, on court order verifying sex reassignment surgery and name change. Driver's licences carried an X sex descriptor from December 2010, but the Department of Finance and Administration rescinded X descriptors in March 2024.

State-level legal protections for gender identity are thin. Arkansas law does not address discrimination based on gender identity; protection exists only through the 2020 Bostock v. Clayton County nationwide ban. Arkansas has no hate-crime penalty-enhancement statute, and its civil remedy for intimidation, harassment, violence or property damage covers only racial, religious or ethnic animosity, not gender identity. Federal law covers gender identity since October 2009 under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Act, but the April 2021 Arkansas state hate-crimes law explicitly excludes sexual orientation and gender identity. Medical practitioners may cite religious beliefs to deny healthcare to LGBT patients under SB 289, signed 26 March and effective immediately.

Local protections are preempted. The Intrastate Commerce Improvement Act (Act 137, enacted 24 February 2015) bars cities and counties from adopting or enforcing ordinances creating protected classifications not contained in state law, which does not include gender identity. The Arkansas Supreme Court applied this in February 2017 to invalidate Fayetteville's non-discrimination ordinance covering employment, housing and public accommodations. Little Rock, Conway, Hot Springs, North Little Rock and Pulaski County bar gender-identity discrimination in public employment, but Eureka Springs and Fayetteville's comprehensive ordinances are unenforced under the Act.

Custody and detention carry documented harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies for transgender inmates that mandate cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy; imprisoned transgender people reported denied care, and the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025. In immigration detention, transgender men faced forced-labour programmes, beatings, solitary confinement and widespread sexual abuse.

Official hostility extends to enforcement machinery. In December 2025 the attorney general instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists promoting what she called radical gender ideology, describing such activists as domestic terrorist groups. A May 2026 national counterterrorism strategy stated that counterterrorism activity would prioritise the rapid identification and neutralisation of groups described as anti-American, radically pro-transgender and anarchist.

Entry screening carries its own exposure. On 5 February 2025 an executive order titled "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports" was issued, and on 25 February 2025 the State Department announced it would bar trans athletes from entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating as fraud, with a permanent bar, any applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth. The Transportation Security Administration's checkpoint procedures involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can be invasive of privacy and risk outing a trans traveller.

Several federal measures remain in litigation. The military purge under Executive Order 14183, the women's sports ban under Executive Order 14201, a January 2025 federal funding freeze, and an October 2025 rule blocking student loan forgiveness for public workers who provide gender-affirming care to transgender youth are all blocked, enjoined, or contested in court, so the operative position on any given measure should be checked before travel.
tangentialFactors:
Arkansas's placement in the "Worst Policies In Effect" tier of the July 2026 risk map sits one level below the four "Do Not Travel" states (Florida, Idaho, Kansas, Texas), whose escalation was driven by Idaho's felony bathroom ban (up to 5 years, partially court-blocked but in force wherever no gender-neutral option exists) and Kansas's bounty-hunter civil-suit regime. Arkansas has not adopted comparable felony penalties or civil bounty regimes, but its cluster of misdemeanour-level facilities restrictions, sports bans, and care bans places it in the same high-risk grouping as Alabama, Indiana, Louisiana, Mississippi, Ohio, Oklahoma, North Dakota, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, West Virginia and Wyoming.

Arkansas's care ban follows the national pattern: gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, and Arkansas was the first to enact such a ban. Its facilities restrictions also follow a national pattern, with bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and, in some states, government buildings covering 9 states and 1 territory, while 29 states, 4 territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban.

The Eighth Circuit's August 2025 reversal of the Arkansas care-ban injunction aligns Arkansas with the Supreme Court's reasoning in United States v. Skrmetti and signals that federal appellate courts are willing to permit state-level care restrictions to take effect, a trend that distinguishes Arkansas from jurisdictions where such bans remain enjoined.

The Intrastate Commerce Improvement Act's preemption of local non-discrimination ordinances mirrors a broader state-level strategy of stripping municipal authority over protected classifications, limiting the ability of Arkansas cities to offer protections the state itself withholds.
